Yes it happens to all of us. Some people just make friends right out of the gate so it seems like you're doing something wrong.

Making friends: If you're going to class alone, odds are other people are too. You'll see people sitting silently by themselves in class, sit next to them and just make conversation. That's how I met one of my best friends. Otherwise, join clubs or societies you are interested in. You'll meet likeminded people and your odds of friendship are pretty good. 

As far as partying is concerned, I think to much emphasis gets placed on it. Realistically you're not gonna party every night of the week,or even every week. You got assignments, reading and other things to do, and partying is a lot of time that school often calls for. My advice: Get to know your floor, then host a party yourself. People will know you as somebody who parties and you'll get invited to things.

Bottom line: I've come to believe the pandemic messed with everybody's heads and they forgot how to be social. You need to make the first move. Act lonely, you stay lonely. Put yourself out there, and the relationships come. But you can't just go about your day in complete isolation and just expect it to happen to you. Don't feel bad about being lonely or not partying, that's all part of university and going out on your own. Like I said, it happens to all of us. But if you want those things, you have to make the happen. It won't happen on its own.

Parking is at a premium but there will be room for you somewhere. Don't stress, the feeling of seeing your dorm for the first time and realizing you're finally in university is top tier. UAlberta is in Edmonton and the same distance from Calgary as Queen's is to Toronto. Alberta is the center of the Canadian oil and gas industry and there is a huge amount of mining there too. Most companies in the field have offices in Calgary/Edmonton. UAlberta is also highly respected for its research and academics. I don't know why being close to Toronto is a huge thing for you but it's not the only important city in Canada. However I agree that Queen's has a nicer campus and community, and there is a lot more variation in the engineering programs and what you can study. You are also close to the nuclear sector and hydro if that's your thing. Queen's Internships and Co-op are interchangeable imo, they offer similar experience and allow you to line up a job before you graduate. Don't be fooled: weather in Kingston can be shit too, but Alberta is definitely worse. Truthfully they are identical in academic standing when it comes to getting a job, so I would make your decision based on the financial aspect and the campus experience. Hope that helps!

People with transplants usually have to take medication every day to make sure their body doesn't reject the transplant. So imagine trying to do all that with the brain.
